nameStory: The Baltimore Snout gets its name from the city of Baltimore, Maryland, where early specimens were likely collected and described by French entomologist Achille Guenée in 1854. The 'snout' part refers to the moth's prominent forward-projecting mouthparts called palps, which stick out like a little nose or snout from the front of its head.
description: The Baltimore Snout is a medium-sized brown moth with distinctive forward-projecting mouthparts that give it a 'snouted' appearance. These moths have mottled brown and gray wings with subtle patterns that help them blend in with tree bark and dead leaves. They're part of the large Erebidae family, which includes many nocturnal moths. Adults typically have a wingspan of about 1 to 1.5 inches across.

idTips.label: Projecting snout
idTips.description: Look for the obvious forward-pointing palps (mouthparts) that extend like a small beak or snout from the front of the head - this is the most distinctive feature

idTips.label: Wing pattern
idTips.description: Wings are mottled brown and gray with subtle wavy lines and darker patches that feel rough to the touch when gently handled

idTips.label: Resting position
idTips.description: When at rest, holds wings in a triangular tent-like shape over the body, with the snout pointing forward

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Medium-sized with a sturdy, compact body and wingspan typically around 1 to 1.5 inches - about the size of a quarter when wings are spread

idTips.label: Coloration
idTips.description: Overall brownish-gray appearance with no bright colors - designed to blend in with bark and dried vegetation

habitat: Baltimore Snouts are found in woodlands, forest edges, parks, and suburban areas with plenty of trees and shrubs throughout New England. They're particularly common around deciduous forests and mixed woodland areas where their caterpillars can feed on various plants. You'll often spot adults around outdoor lights at night or resting on tree trunks and wooden structures during the day.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in April and May from overwintering pupae. Look for them around porch lights and outdoor lighting on warm evenings.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with multiple generations flying. Adults are most commonly seen from June through August, attracted to lights and occasionally found resting on tree bark during the day.
seasonality.fall: Second and sometimes third generation adults continue flying well into October. Late-season individuals may appear more worn with faded wing patterns.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not active. The species overwinters as pupae hidden in leaf litter and soil, preparing for the next year's emergence.

funFact: Baltimore Snouts are like the marathon runners of the moth world - they can have at least two complete generations in New England each year, with southern populations squeezing in even more generations, meaning great-grandparent and great-grandchild moths might be flying in the same calendar year!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other snout moths in the same genus, but the Baltimore Snout's brownish coloration and specific wing pattern help distinguish it. Remember: if it has a prominent snout and looks like tree bark, check the overall brown coloration rather than green tones to separate it from its Green Cloverworm Moth cousin.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name includes 'baltimoralis' referring to Baltimore, but these moths are found far beyond Maryland throughout much of eastern North America. Despite being called 'snout' moths, the projecting parts aren't actually a nose but modified mouthparts used for feeding and sensing their environment.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Green Cloverworm Moth, the Baltimore Snout is more brownish rather than greenish and has different wing markings. Both species share the characteristic forward-projecting snout, but the Green Cloverworm Moth tends to have more olive or greenish tones in its coloration. The Baltimore Snout's wings also tend to have more distinct mottled patterns compared to the more uniform coloration of its green cousin.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Green Cloverworm Moth is larger and more robust than its close relative the Baltimore Snout, which tends to be smaller and more delicate-looking.
